title: Genere degli Articoli e dei Sostantivi
subtitle: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine — and the article always agrees.
objectives: Identify whether a noun is masculine or feminine from its ending
Choose the correct definite article (il, lo, la, l', i, gli, le)
Choose the correct indefinite article (un, uno, una, un')

content.intro: In Italian, every noun — even for objects with no natural gender, like a table or a book — is grammatically masculine or feminine, and every article that points to it must agree.
content.explanation: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (il libro, the book) and most ending in -a are feminine (la casa, the house). Nouns ending in -e can be either gender and simply have to be learned (il pane is masculine, la notte is feminine). The article you use depends on both the noun's gender and the sound it starts with.

rules.heading: a) Definite article ("the") — singular
rules.body:
• il — masculine + consonant: il libro
  • lo — masculine + s+consonant, z, gn, ps, y: lo studente, lo zaino
  • l' — masculine or feminine + vowel: l'amico, l'amica
  • la — feminine + consonant: la casa

rules.heading: b) Definite article — plural
rules.body:
• i — plural of il: i libri
  • gli — plural of lo and of l' (masculine): gli studenti, gli amici
  • le — plural of la and l' (feminine): le case, le amiche

rules.heading: c) Indefinite article ("a/an")
rules.body:
• un — masculine + consonant or vowel: un libro, un amico
  • uno — masculine + s+consonant, z, gn: uno studente, uno zaino
  • una — feminine + consonant: una casa
  • un' — feminine + vowel (with apostrophe): un'amica

rules.heading: d) Forming the plural
rules.body:
• -o → -i: libro → libri
  • -a → -e: casa → case
  • -e → -i (both genders): notte → notti, pane → pani

examples.en: The book is on the table.
I have a [female] friend in Rome.
The student studies in the library.
The students are good [at what they do].

examples.it: Le case in questa via sono antiche.
examples.en: The houses on this street are old.
A new backpack costs a lot.

commonMistakes.why: Before a vowel, il/lo shorten to l' — il amico is never used.
Masculine nouns starting with z take lo, not il.
The apostrophe form un' is only for feminine nouns before a vowel; masculine amico takes plain un.
Plural masculine nouns need the plural article i (or gli), never the feminine la.

exercises.title: Fill in the Correct Article
exercises.instructions: Complete each phrase with il, lo, la, or l'.

items.explanation: Masculine nouns starting with s+consonant take lo.
Before a vowel, the feminine article shortens to l'.
Pane is masculine and starts with a consonant, so it takes il.
Notte is feminine (despite the -e ending) and starts with a consonant.

items.prompt: What is the plural of "lo zaino"?
items.explanation: Gli is the plural of lo.

items.prompt: What is the plural of "la casa"?
items.explanation: Feminine -a nouns become -e in the plural, with the article le.
Before a vowel, il shortens to l'.
Before a vowel, feminine una becomes un', with an apostrophe.

summary: Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine; -a usually feminine; -e can be either and must be learned.
Definite articles: il/lo/l' (m. sing.), la/l' (f. sing.), i/gli (m. pl.), le (f. pl.) — chosen by gender and starting sound.
Indefinite articles: un/uno (m.), una/un' (f.) — un' only before a feminine vowel.
